What does a lethal dose of radiation actually do to the human body, hour by hour?

In 1958, Los Alamos worker Cecil Kelley was standing beside a plutonium processing tank when it suddenly went critical. In less than a fraction of a second, he was blasted with an enormous dose of neutron and gamma radiation. At first, the damage was almost invisible. Within minutes, Kelley became confused, collapsed, began vomiting, and developed severe skin redness. His blood pressure crashed, his body started swelling, and his nervous system began to fail.
Then something strange happened. He appeared to get better. The vomiting stopped. He became lucid. His temperature returned to normal. But inside his body, the systems keeping him alive were shutting down. His lymphocytes disappeared, his bone marrow was almost completely destroyed, his blood vessels began leaking fluid, and the rapidly renewing tissue inside his digestive system could no longer replace itself.

description:
The Colorado River is running out of water, and the fight over who gets what could reshape the American West.

This video explores why the crisis is far more complicated than shorter showers, dry lawns, or growing desert cities. Agriculture consumes the largest share of Colorado River water, with enormous amounts going toward crops like alfalfa and hay. Some of that feed is then exported overseas, effectively shipping scarce Western water out of the country. But the deeper problem goes back more than a century.

The 1922 Colorado River Compact divided up more water than the river reliably produces. Today, shrinking snowpack, rising temperatures, and decades of overuse have pushed Lake Mead and Lake Powell toward dangerously low levels. Now the legal battle is intensifying. Arizona faces much deeper cuts than California because of decades-old water agreements and the doctrine of prior appropriation.
